clue.text: First of the chickens moulting as programmes finishing once (7,4)

indicators.note: Asking for the first of something takes only the letter standing at the front of the word that follows.

blocks.note: the letter the bird's name opens with
a moulting bird is shedding the soft feathers underneath, so it is losing its down

annotation.surface: Hens shedding their feathers while the evening's television programmes come to an end.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Moulting' looks like an instruction to shuffle letters and is a plain synonym instead. 'Once' points at the years when British channels shut for the night rather than running on until dawn.
annotation.definitionFit: Closing down is what a channel does when its programmes stop for the night, from the era when broadcasting ended before midnight.

clue.text: Finish one’s sentence and heed driving instructor (4,2,1,4,4)

blocks.note: the punctuation reading: the dot that every written sentence ends on
the traffic reading: what a learner is told to do at a junction, wheels not moving at all

annotation.surface: Somebody being told both to finish what they are saying and to obey the man in the passenger seat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Full stop' is a mark of punctuation in one reading and a complete halt in the other, and the 'and' invites you to read the whole line as one sentence rather than as two separate demands.
annotation.definitionFit: A sentence ends at a full stop, and a driving instructor asks for one at a junction — the punctuation mark and the dead halt share the phrase.

clue.text: Invigorating air in Gozo? Never! (5)

indicators.note: The little word says the letters are sitting inside what comes next rather than being described by it.

blocks.note: five letters in an unbroken run out of the island's name into the word after it, the question mark counting for nothing

annotation.surface: Somebody scoffing at the suggestion that the air on a Maltese island is bracing.
annotation.walkthrough: Gozo is the smaller of Malta's two inhabited islands, and the indignant 'Never!' keeps you reading the line as an argument instead of as a place to look.
annotation.definitionFit: Ozone is the gas, but in everyday British use it is the sharp seaside tang people say is doing them good.

clue.text: Sick notes lead to notoriety (3,4)

blocks.note: sick and ill are the same complaint
fa and me are two of the sol-fa notes, sung in that order

annotation.surface: A pile of doctor's certificates that ends up making somebody notorious.
annotation.walkthrough: Sol-fa hands crosswords a whole scale of tiny words — do, re, me, fa, so, la, te — and two of them run together here, which is why the plural 'notes' matters.
annotation.definitionFit: A house of ill fame is a brothel, and ill fame on its own is the bad reputation itself, a noun that swaps straight in for notoriety.

clue.text: Band’s origin (7)

blocks.note: the rock group Peter Gabriel and Phil Collins fronted took this word as its name
the plain sense: the beginning of something, the point it started from

annotation.surface: The story of where a rock group got started.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s reads as a possessive and is doing nothing of the kind — it is the equals sign between two meanings, one of them the Bible's opening book, which is why beginnings carry its name.
annotation.definitionFit: The Bible's first book gives the word its sense of a beginning, and the rock group took it as a name, so 'Band' defines by example.

clue.text: Islander’s love of pastoral life lacks initial attractiveness (8)

indicators.note: What a word lacks is missing from it, so the letter named next never gets written down.
'Initial' picks out the letter a word starts with, here to say which single letter is the one to go.

blocks.note: love is nothing on a tennis scoreboard, and nothing is written as a nought
Arcadian means belonging to an idealised country life, and it arrives here short of its opening letter
the A that this word begins with is the letter taken away

annotation.surface: An islander whose fondness for the simple country life does not look appealing to begin with.
annotation.walkthrough: Arcadia was a mountainous district of Greece that poets turned into shorthand for shepherds and simplicity, so 'pastoral life' is doing the work of a place name here.
annotation.definitionFit: An Orcadian is a native of Orkney, the islands off the north coast of Scotland, so 'islander' names the person by where they come from.

clue.text: Windies won – Kent gets caught out, when the last man is batting (4,7,4)

definitions.text: when the last man is batting

indicators.note: 'Out' here is not the cricketer's dismissal but the sense of out of order, so the letters beside it do not stay as printed.

blocks.note: fourteen letters of raw material: the Windies are the West Indies cricket team and Kent an English county side
c is what a scorer writes for caught, beside the fielder's name

annotation.surface: A match report in which the West Indies beat Kent and a Kent player is caught.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface is cricket, which is where the definition hides too: a side has eleven batters, so nine of them already dismissed leaves the last man at the crease.
annotation.definitionFit: Nine wickets down means nine of the eleven batters are out, and the eleventh — the last man — is the one still batting.

clue.text: Letter to boy questionable help getting Botham as US citizen (13)

indicators.note: Something questionable is not to be taken as it stands, and neither is the printed order of the four letters beside it.

blocks.note: phi is a letter of the Greek alphabet, the one that gives us physics and philosophy
a lad is a boy
the same four letters in another order
Ian Botham, England's great cricket all-rounder, hands over his first name

annotation.surface: Dubious assistance with a letter to a boy, somehow involving a famous cricketer.
annotation.walkthrough: Greek letters are the crossword's spare alphabet — phi, chi, psi, eta — so 'Letter' asks for one of those rather than for something posted, and a surname alone is enough to summon a forename.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone from Philadelphia is a US citizen, so the definition works by example: one city's residents standing in for Americans at large.

clue.text: It’s deteriorated a lot, sadly wasn’t over here (5,4,4)

indicators.note: Read as 'in a sorry state' rather than as the speaker's regret, and letters in a sorry state have fallen out of the order they were given in.

blocks.note: thirteen letters of raw material, the apostrophe ignored

annotation.surface: A regretful report that something has gone downhill and was not on this side of the water.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma does the hiding: read straight on past it and 'sadly' looks like the speaker's regret rather than the instruction governing the three words after it.
annotation.definitionFit: The phrase is the superlative complaint — the state of a thing that has now declined further than at any point before.

clue.text: Poor actor’s part as expressed on picnic menu (3,4)

definitions.note: The setter defines by where the thing is found rather than with a synonym, so the definition is a phrase off the menu card and not words you could swap for the answer.

indicators.note: Expressed means said out loud, so what counts about the word before it is its sound and not its spelling.

blocks.note: a ham is an actor who overplays every line
an actor's part is a role, and that sound is spelt another way in a baker's window

annotation.surface: An overacted part being declaimed while somebody reads what is on offer for the picnic.
annotation.walkthrough: Both food words in the answer are theatre words first: the ham is the actor and the part is his role, and only the sound of the second one ever reaches the picnic basket.
annotation.definitionFit: A ham roll is the filled bread roll of every buffet, which is why the setter points at the menu it appears on rather than at a synonym.

clue.text: Bottle party? (2,3,2)

blocks.note: at this sort of party the drink turns up in bottles, so the tin is the thing the room has none of
a do is a party, from a works do to a big do

annotation.surface: An invitation to the kind of party where every guest brings a bottle.
annotation.walkthrough: Both words work twice over, and the joke is about the answer's own syllables rather than its meaning: a party supplied with bottles is a do at which the other container is missing. Nothing here defines the flat refusal the phrase normally is.
annotation.definitionFit: A bottle party is a do where guests bring their own bottles, so the clue names the answer by reading its words literally instead of by its sense of refusal.

clue.text: Martin’s followers reform most of unearthly beliefs ultimately (9)

indicators.note: To re-form a thing is to form it again in a different shape, which is what happens to the letters it governs.
Most of a word is all of it bar the end, so its final letter is left behind before anything else happens.
'Ultimately' points at the very end of the word before it, meaning its last letter and nothing more.

blocks.note: eight of that word's nine letters, the tail one dropped
the letter that word finishes on

annotation.surface: A congregation finally overhauling most of its unearthly doctrine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reform' is the joke as well as the instruction: the Martin whose followers these are set the Reformation going, and only a first name is needed to name him.
annotation.definitionFit: Martin Luther's followers are the members of the Protestant church founded on his teaching, so the plural definition names the people rather than the creed.

clue.text: They’re not here, but are in Sussex and Hampshire (5)

blocks.note: the puzzle talking about itself: in an across entry, the clues running the other way are the ones not in this row
the chalk hill ranges that roll through both of those southern counties carry the word as their name

annotation.surface: A claim that certain things are absent from here but present in two southern counties.
annotation.walkthrough: One half of this is a crossword being cheeky about its own grid, which is why 'not here' has to be read as a position on the page; the other half is ordinary English geography.
annotation.definitionFit: The Downs are the chalk hills of southern England, and in solvers' shorthand the downs are the clues running vertically — the ones this row does not hold.

clue.text: College official – idle, vain, absent now and again (4)

indicators.note: Letters absent now and again means every other one has gone missing, so you read only the ones still standing.

blocks.note: the second and fourth letters of each of the two words, taken in turn

annotation.surface: A college officer accused of being lazy, conceited and never at his desk.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Absent' reads as a third failing in the list and is half the instruction instead: it says letters go missing, and 'now and again' says how often they do it.
annotation.definitionFit: A dean heads a college faculty or a cathedral chapter, so the definition names an office rather than describing the person holding it.

clue.text: Welsh girl about to be cuddled by cute pedigree pet (7,3)

indicators.note: Being cuddled by something means being wrapped up in its arms, so those letters close around whatever is named before them.

blocks.note: pert is cute in the cheeky, saucy sense, and it opens up to take the other pieces
Siân is the Welsh form of Jane and a common girl's name in Wales
ca. is short for circa, the 'about' written in front of a date nobody can pin down

annotation.surface: A Welsh girl being cuddled by an adorable pedigree animal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cute' reads as part of the description of the animal and belongs to the wordplay instead, which leaves only two words to define with — and both of them are true of a whole family of breeds.
annotation.definitionFit: A Persian cat is one long-haired pedigree breed, so 'pedigree pet' defines by example: one of the animals a cat show is full of.

clue.text: F. Gump actor cuts toe, because of … ? (6,2)

indicators.note: To cut a word is to shorten it, and this one does the job twice over, on the name in front of it and on the word after.

blocks.note: Tom Hanks played Forrest Gump, and the forename is cut back to its initial in front of the surname
the same knife takes the last letter off the toe

annotation.surface: Somebody explaining how the star of Forrest Gump came to cut his toe, then trailing off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cuts toe' reads as an accident in the surface and is a pair of instructions underneath. The trailing dots leave the sentence hanging, which is how a definition that normally opens a phrase can sit at the end of one.
annotation.definitionFit: Thanks to something is because of it — the phrase works for a cause of good fortune and, just as often, ironically for the cause of a mishap.

clue.text: Rude hallo I might produce? (4-6)

indicators.note: What is produced comes out unlike the stuff it was made from, so the letters named are free to arrive in a new order.

blocks.note: ten letters, taken exactly as printed before anything is done to them

annotation.surface: An impolite greeting somebody is threatening to deliver.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word does both jobs at once: read straight, the line is the gadget boasting about the noise it can make; read as instructions, those same ten letters spell it. The question mark is the setter admitting it.
annotation.definitionFit: A loud-hailer is the hand-held megaphone that turns a shout into a bellow, so a rude hallo is precisely what one might produce.

clue.text: Sharon, say, is PM, losing head (7)

indicators.note: The head of a word is the letter at its front, and losing it means starting one letter further in.

blocks.note: Benjamin Disraeli was Queen Victoria's prime minister, so two letters call up his whole name

annotation.surface: A prime minister called Sharon losing her head over something.
annotation.walkthrough: Sharon reads as an English woman's first name and is Ariel Sharon, who led Israel — 'say' flagging him as an example. A second prime minister is hiding behind the two letters PM.
annotation.definitionFit: Ariel Sharon led Israel as its prime minister, so he is one instance of the nationality the answer names, which is what 'say' marks.

clue.text: Land collapsing into sea (7)

indicators.note: Anything that collapses falls in on itself and keeps none of its shape, and neither do the letters after it.

blocks.note: seven letters, the two little words taken together as raw material

annotation.surface: A stretch of coastline crumbling into the water.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Into sea' reads as where the falling land is going and is the raw material instead, which leaves exactly one word to do the defining.
annotation.definitionFit: Estonia is a country on the Baltic, and 'land' is the plainest word there is for a country, defining it by its category.

clue.text: Regularly – often – tea is cheese (4)

indicators.note: Taken regularly means taken at a fixed interval — every second letter of what follows, and none of the ones between.

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of the two words read as one run

annotation.surface: Somebody remarking that their tea is regularly nothing but cheese.
annotation.walkthrough: Tea across much of Britain is the evening meal rather than the drink, which is what makes a sentence about cheese sound like an ordinary complaint. The dashes are decoration.
annotation.definitionFit: Feta is the white, salty Greek cheese kept in brine, so the single word names it by the family it belongs to.

clue.text: Beauty captured by the lens (5)

indicators.note: What is captured is held inside its captor, so the letters are prisoners of the words that follow.

blocks.note: five consecutive letters running out of one word into the next

annotation.surface: A beautiful subject caught by a photographer's camera.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Captured by the lens' is photography in the surface and imprisonment underneath, and the answer is a name doing duty as a common noun.
annotation.definitionFit: Helen of Troy is the standard example of a beauty, the face that launched a thousand ships, so the noun names her by what she is famous for.

clue.text: Trousers, lost at the start, eventually turned up (9)

indicators.note: Something lost has wandered off from where it belongs, and letters that have wandered do not come back in order.
The start of a word is the single letter it opens with, and that letter is all this asks for.

blocks.note: eight letters of raw material, the garment itself playing no part
the letter that word begins with

annotation.surface: Trousers mislaid early on and found at last with their hems folded over.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turned up' is a hem in the surface and a nose in the answer, which is the French word English keeps for a nose tilted at the tip.
annotation.definitionFit: Retroussé describes a nose tipped up at its end, and 'turned up' is the plain English adjective for exactly that shape.

clue.text: Orchids, originally unaltered, an ikebana requirement? (5)

indicators.note: The origin of a word is the letter it begins with, and that opening letter is all it hands over.

blocks.note: the letter the flower's name starts with
something left unaltered is left as is, and those two words run together

annotation.surface: Orchids kept exactly as they came, and what a Japanese flower arrangement needs.
annotation.walkthrough: Ikebana is the Japanese art of flower arranging, and what it needs is the florist's block of green foam that holds stems where they are put — not the desert waterhole the orchids are steering you towards.
annotation.definitionFit: Oasis is the trade name of the water-holding foam florists push stems into, so an arrangement needs one — the question mark flags the brand.

clue.text: Tastier dancing from this performer? (7)

indicators.note: A dancer never stays in the same place for long, and neither do the letters standing beside the word.

blocks.note: the seven letters of the fodder, exactly as printed

annotation.surface: Dancing in better taste than usual, from the entertainer responsible for it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'This performer' points back at the fodder rather than forward at anything new: the more tasteful dancing comes out of those very letters, which is what the question mark acknowledges.
annotation.definitionFit: An artiste is a professional entertainer — singer, dancer, circus turn — the French spelling English keeps when 'performer' wants a little glamour.

clue.text: Duck. On reflection, 20! (2,5)

indicators.note: A reflection shows a thing the other way round, so the two letters in front of it are written back to front.

blocks.note: two letters taken as printed, then turned round
a score is twenty, as in three score years and ten

annotation.surface: Somebody thinking again and settling on the number twenty.
annotation.walkthrough: '20' looks like a cross-reference to the clue numbered 20 and is the plain number instead. A duck in cricket is a batter dismissed without troubling the scorers, named after the duck's egg a nought resembles.
annotation.definitionFit: Duck is cricket's word for an innings that ends without a single run, so it is precisely a nought on the scoreboard.

clue.text: NT character making drop-goals in error (8,3)

indicators.note: Something written in error has come out wrong, and these letters have come out in the wrong order.

blocks.note: eleven letters of raw material, the hyphen and the little word included

annotation.surface: A rugby player whose attempts at drop-goals keep going wrong.
annotation.walkthrough: NT is the New Testament, and the parable behind the phrase is the one about the son who spends his inheritance and comes home to a feast. 'In error' reads as the player's mistake and is the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: The prodigal son is the wastrel of Jesus's parable in Luke, so 'NT character' names him as one figure out of the New Testament.
